human_tolerance.notes: Depends on large trees for nesting, so where an area is extensively deforested it only uses gardens occasionally and is not present in numbers; it drums on hollow trees and also on aluminium roofs, metal guttering and transformer boxes in urban environments, and both sexes dig their own nest cavity.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: The species excavates cavities for nesting and roosting, holds them the year round, and marks the area around nest sites with drilling holes to warn others away.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: 'In early May, the red-bellied woodpeckers begin breeding activities by drumming patterns, such as slow taps followed by short rapid drumming.' The end date is judgement; the article gives no dates past the start.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: Both sexes dig the nesting cavity in a dead tree, an old stump or a softwood live tree such as elm, maple or willow; the male locates the hole and seeks his mate's approval by mutual tapping, and the female accepts by completing the excavation. The juvenile is ready to fledge at 24-26 days.

phases.name: caching
phases.note: Hides berries and acorns deep in natural crevices to keep them from interspecific competitors.

phases.name: young
phases.note: The juvenile remains in its natal area for about 27 weeks after fledging, and natal dispersal has been observed; it may return to breed there, depending on predation levels and food.

vocalizations.description: Red-bellied woodpeckers are noisy birds with many varied calls, described as sounding like churr-churr-churr or thrraa-thrraa-thrraa with an alternating br-r-r-r-t sound. Males call and drum more often than females, but both sexes call.
A loud chee-wuck, chee-wuck, chee-wuck given in an intraspecific conflict, such as two birds competing for the same mate, accompanied by drumming with the bill.
Drumming with the bill on hollow trees, and on metal objects in towns, which sounds like six taps; used to attract mates, to maintain pair bonding and in conflict.

One of a varied repertoire of loud rattling calls, given by both sexes through the year and used to keep a pair together; the drumming itself - slow taps followed by short rapid drumming - carries much of the same message.
A harsh alarm call, given either while hiding from a predator or while harassing it.

The running commentary of the species: a 'churr-churr-churr' or 'thrraa-thrraa-thrraa' with an alternating br-r-r-r-t sound. Red-bellied woodpeckers are noisy birds with many varied calls, and both sexes give them.
A loud repeated 'chee-wuck, chee-wuck, chee-wuck', given in an intraspecific conflict such as two males competing for the same mate, and used to harass an approaching predator.
A low 'grr, grr' exchanged by a pair from the start of courtship until the end of the breeding season.
The high-pitched begging call of a nestling, continued for some time after fledging whenever the young bird sees its parents.

taxonomy.note: The species is monotypic: no subspecies are recognised.

external.note: iNaturalist, NCBI and eBird ids via Wikidata P3151, P685 and P3444.

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = least concern (Q211005); 'Though the species is not globally threatened, it depends on large trees for nesting.'

range.note: Breeds mainly in the eastern United States, ranging as far south as Florida and as far north as Canada.

traits.limb_count.note: Biped: two legs; the wings are not counted as limbs.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Clings to and hops up tree trunks, tapping and drilling, and flies between trees; the schema has no Climb-to-pose mapping, so Hop and Fly are the modes recorded here.

traits.nest_type.note: 'They nest in the decayed cavities of dead trees, old stumps, or in live trees that have softer wood such as elms, maples, or willows; both sexes assist in digging nesting cavities.'

traits.perching.note: Clings to trunks and branches to work the bark and to hammer stored food into crevices.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Judgement, not sourced. No openly licensed source used in this record gives a longevity figure for the red-bellied woodpecker, and the Wikipedia article gives none. 9.2 years is an authored placeholder on the scale of a large woodpecker and should be treated as unverified.

traits.diet.note: 'These birds mainly search out arthropods on tree trunks. They rarely catch insects in flight. They are omnivores, eating insects, fruits, nuts and seeds.' The 60/20/20 split is judgement; the occasional consumption of box-duck eggs is noted qualitatively and not modelled.

traits.social.note: 'the red-bellied woodpecker is known to be in monogamous relationships', with the male locating the nest hole and the female accepting it by completing the excavation.

traits.activity_pattern.note: EltonTraits Nocturnal 0; Wikipedia describes a bird that calls and drums through the day in every season.

traits.defense.note: 'They defend their nests and young aggressively, and may directly attack predators that come near the nest'; mapped to Mob.

traits.wariness.note: Dares to drum on roofs, guttering and transformer boxes in towns, though it needs large trees and so is patchy in built-up areas.

habitat.use.note: Almost all its time is on trunks, branches and canopy; the small ground share reflects occasional feeding low in a tree.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Excavates and roosts in its own cavities.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow traits.diet; nest and roost cavities from the nesting description.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: 'In areas that are extensively deforested, the birds will sometimes utilize gardens', and it taps on 'aluminum roofs, metal guttering and transformer boxes in urban environments'.

seasonal.strategy.note: No migration is described and it holds cavity territories year-round, so ActiveYearRound is used; the article does not discuss movements.

seasonal.phases.note: 'In early May, the red-bellied woodpeckers begin breeding activities', which fixes the start; the end date is authored because the article gives none. Year-round cavity use and drilling-marked nest sites are described in the ecology section.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Nestlings give a high-pitched begging call that continues after fledging, but the article gives no incubation or fledgling age, so the Juvenile stage carries no duration.

look.note: Light grey face and underparts with black-and-white barring on back, wings and tail, a vivid orange-red crown and nape on the male (red nape and forehead patch on the female), and a pale reddish tinge on the lower belly that gives the species its name; the crown and back barring are extra parts and the proportions are authored judgement.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program, which is the closest shared program for a woodpecker that perches, drums, roosts in a cavity and forages by hopping. food_tag invertebrate matches the arthropod diet; flee_m 12 m is longer than for a small songbird because the bird is large and defends its nest aggressively. The program's song slot is wired to this species' general contact call, because its drumming and contact calls are what the sources document.

vocalizations.contact_call.note: Wikipedia describes this species as noisy with many varied calls, and gives the drumming pattern that precedes breeding; the specific call wording and the cooldown are authored. No open source gives frequency bands, so freq_hz is omitted.

vocalizations.alarm_call.note: Wikipedia states it hides from a predator or harasses it with alarm calls; the wording and the cooldown are authored.

habitat.density_per_ha.note: Judgement: no open source gives a density. A woodpecker pair holding a year-round territory in mature deciduous forest with snags works on a multi-hectare territory, giving typical 0.15 per hectare, and min and max are an authored tenfold band either side, following the convention used for turdus-migratorius and cardinalis-cardinalis.

vocalizations.note: The churr and thrraa calls, the six-tap drumming on hollow trees and on roofs, gutters and transformer boxes, the loud 'chee-wuck' conflict and harassment call, the low pair 'grr, grr' from courtship to the end of breeding, and the high-pitched 'pree-pree-pree' nestling beg continued after fledging are all quoted or closely paraphrased from the article's Vocalizations, Behavior and ecology and Breeding sections. Cooldowns are authored judgement; no open source quantifies them. No open source gives frequency bands, so freq_hz is omitted.
